lesson.title: Poison Reverse: Saying Unreachable Out Loud Instead of Staying Silent
lesson.summary: Poison reverse strengthens split horizon by having a router actively advertise a route back to the neighbor it learned it from, but with a cost of infinity, making the do not route through me message explicit instead of just leaving it unsaid.
lesson.body:
Split horizon fixes the count to infinity problem in the A, B, C example by having C simply say nothing about A when talking to B. Poison reverse takes the same underlying insight, C's route to A goes through B, so B does not need it from C, and expresses it differently: rather than omitting the route, C still includes A in its advertisement to B, but lists the distance as infinity, 16 in RIP's terms. The practical effect is the same as split horizon, B will not learn a usable route to A from C, but the mechanism is a positive, explicit statement instead of a silence.

That difference in mechanism matters more than it might first appear. Silence is ambiguous: if an expected route is simply missing from an update, a router cannot always immediately tell whether the neighbor genuinely has no route, whether the update was dropped in transit, or whether it just has not arrived yet. An explicit cost of infinity removes that ambiguity, it is a direct, unmistakable statement that this path does not exist, use something else. In practice this can help a router recognize and react to a broken route slightly faster and more reliably than relying purely on absence.

Poison reverse shares split horizon's core limitation, though, and it is worth being honest about it: it still only prevents the immediate, two router loop between a router and the exact neighbor it learned a route from. In a topology involving three or more routers whose routes to some destination form a longer cycle, stale information can still circulate along a path that never triggers any single router's poison reverse rule, because poison reverse only fires between a route's source neighbor and the router advertising back to it, not across the whole loop. Poison reverse also has a real cost: advertising every route back to its source, even as infinity, makes update messages larger, which matters more in bigger networks. In practice, RIP and similar protocols typically combine split horizon with poison reverse and lean on RIP's hop count ceiling as a final backstop, accepting that these techniques substantially shrink the count to infinity problem for the common cases without claiming to eliminate every possible routing loop.
